summary: At dawn after the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary come to the tomb. An earthquake and descending angel expose an empty place and announce that Jesus has been raised ‘just as he said.’ The women leave with fear and great joy to tell the disciples, and Jesus meets them on the way. Guards report to chief priests, who pay for an alternative story. In Galilee the eleven worship and doubt. Jesus declares all authority in heaven and earth, commissions them to make disciples of all nations by going, baptizing, and teaching obedience, and closes with the promise, ‘I am with you always.’
whyItMatters: Matthew ends by joining resurrection evidence, contested explanation, imperfect witnesses, universal mission, and presence. Doubt is not edited out before commissioning. The main command is to make disciples, not merely travel or secure decisions, and Jesus's authority is expressed through baptism, sustained teaching, and a promise that answers Immanuel in chapter 1.

context.author: Anonymous narrator concluding with distinctive guard and Galilee-commission scenes
context.audience: A worshiping yet imperfect community already making disciples across nations
context.setting: A tomb near Jerusalem and a mountain in Galilee
context.literaryForm: Empty-tomb announcement, appearance, counter-report, and commissioning epilogue

keyVerses.text: He is not here, for he has risen, just like he said. Come, see the place where the Lord was lying.
keyVerses.why: Announcement, remembered prediction, and invitation to inspect the place belong together.

keyVerses.text: Jesus came to them and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.
keyVerses.why: The scope of authority answers the Gospel's recurring heaven-and-earth language and grounds the commission.

keyVerses.text: teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen.
keyVerses.why: Matthew closes with obedient teaching under the presence promised by ‘Immanuel.’

questions.question: Who rolled away the stone, and was it to let Jesus out?
questions.answer: Matthew says the angel descends, rolls the stone away, and sits on it; Jesus is already described as raised and absent. The opened tomb lets witnesses see, not the risen Jesus escape. The seated angel turns the sealed instrument of control into a place of announcement.

questions.question: Does ‘he has risen’ mean Jesus raised himself?
questions.answer: The Greek ēgerthē is passive, ‘he was raised,’ often understood as a divine passive naming God's action without repeatedly naming God. English idiom commonly says ‘he has risen.’ Matthew also portrays Jesus as living and acting; the passive emphasizes vindication by the Father rather than explaining resurrection mechanics.

questions.question: Why do fear and great joy coexist?
questions.answer: The women encounter a world-altering event, an angelic command, an empty tomb, and a dangerous task. Matthew does not treat fear as the opposite of faith in every context. Their fear travels with joy and obedience: they run to tell, and Jesus meets them on the way.

questions.question: How should the bribed-guard story be read?
questions.answer: Matthew presents an early counter-explanation and explains why it circulated. The claim that sleeping guards knew disciples stole the body contains its own tension, and priests promise political protection. The scene shows resurrection testimony contested from the beginning; it is Matthew's distinctive apologetic narrative, not independent modern proof by itself.

questions.question: How can the eleven worship and doubt at the same time?
questions.answer: Distazō means hesitate or waver, the word used when Peter is divided on the water. The Greek plural may mean some doubted or describe the group collectively; Matthew does not identify which. Resurrection does not instantly turn disciples into psychologically flawless heroes. Jesus approaches and commissions this worshiping, wavering community.

questions.question: What is the main command in the Great Commission?
questions.answer: The controlling imperative is mathēteusate, ‘make disciples.’ ‘Going,’ ‘baptizing,’ and ‘teaching’ are participles explaining the movement. Mission therefore cannot be reduced to travel or conversion counts; it forms learners among all nations into a baptized life of practicing everything Jesus commanded.

questions.question: What does ‘all nations’ mean for Israel?
questions.answer: Panta ta ethnē includes every people and removes an ethnic boundary from the mission. It does not declare Israel discarded: Matthew's story has moved through Abraham, Israel, David, Torah, prophets, and an Israel-focused mission to this worldwide horizon. Gentiles are discipled through Israel's Messiah, not through erasing his story.

questions.question: Why singular ‘name’ but Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?
questions.answer: Matthew uses singular onoma followed by a threefold coordinated confession. The verse became foundational for Christian trinitarian baptism, though later creeds use more developed vocabulary than Matthew supplies here. The formula joins the three within one baptismal allegiance without pausing to explain later metaphysics.

questions.question: How does ‘I am with you always’ complete the book?
questions.answer: The Greek says ‘all the days’ until the completion of the age, turning an abstract always into day-by-day presence. It answers ‘Immanuel, God with us’ from 1:23 and supports a mission impossible by human strength alone. Matthew ends without an ascension scene, leaving Jesus's promised presence as the final sound.

glossary.def: A learner or apprentice formed through allegiance, baptism, and practiced teaching — not merely an admirer.
Immerse or wash into a named allegiance and gathered identity.
Matthew's horizon of completion, up to which the risen Jesus promises daily presence.
